title: The Intermediate Plateau — Motivation at B1–B2

pts: Progress at intermediate level genuinely does slow in visible, easily-noticed terms, even as real underlying competence continues developing.
Early gains (basic survival communication) are highly visible; later gains (nuance, register range) are subtler and harder to notice day to day.
Naming this pattern explicitly to learners can itself reduce the discouragement it often causes.

v: A piece of each learner’s work from three to six months ago; a new piece on a similar task

items: Before the lesson, find a short piece of each learner’s earlier writing (from the portfolio or notebook).
Set a new task on the same theme, for example ‘My favourite festival’.
When learners have finished, return the older piece.
Learners place the two pieces side by side and underline three things they can now do that they could not do then.
Learners write one sentence beginning ‘I have improved in…’ and share it; tell the class that this is what intermediate progress looks like.
For speaking, compare two phone recordings of the same picture description made months apart.
Support: give a checklist of things to look for (longer sentences, linking words, new vocabulary, fewer repeated words).
Challenge: learners explain which change took the most effort.

blocks.x: Two versions from one learner (written for this book):

lines: September: Diwali is my favourite festival. We light lamps. We eat sweets. It is very nice.
February: Diwali is my favourite festival because the whole street comes alive: every house lights diyas, and my grandmother makes chakli that nobody else can match.
S1: In September I write only short sentences. Now I use ‘because’ and ‘and’ and ‘that’.
T: Yes. And look at ‘comes alive’. You didn’t have that expression before. That is intermediate progress.

body: Purpose: to show that progress continues even when it feels flat. Content: a graph with a dotted line labelled ‘What learners feel’ that flattens at B1, and a solid line labelled ‘What is really developing’ that keeps rising. Style: simple, calm, labelled as well as colour-coded. Board version: two lines on an axis, one flattening, one climbing.

items: Google Drive (free) folders for storing scanned samples by date.

blocks.x: Keep one dated sample per learner per month in a paper folder or at the back of the notebook.

pts: Beginner-level gains unlock entirely new communicative abilities; intermediate gains refine abilities already partially present.
The same amount of underlying learning produces a much less dramatic felt improvement at this stage.
This is a structural feature of language development, not evidence of reduced ability or effort.

v: Board; a short list of beginner and intermediate can-do statements

items: Draw a staircase on the board with big steps labelled with beginner abilities (‘say my name’, ‘order food’, ‘ask the time’).
Beside it, draw a long, gentle ramp labelled with intermediate abilities (‘explain a problem politely’, ‘tell a story with suspense’, ‘disagree without sounding rude’).
Ask: which one feels like faster progress? Why?
Explain that each step on the staircase unlocked a new ability; each metre on the ramp refines abilities learners already have.
Use a cricket analogy: a beginner’s first boundary is dramatic; an experienced batter improving footwork improves just as much, but nobody cheers.
Support: prepare cards with abilities for learners to place on the staircase or the ramp.
Challenge: learners explain the idea in writing to a younger learner.

lines: T: When you first learnt ‘Can I have…?’, you could suddenly buy things in English. Now you are learning ‘Would you mind if I…?’. You could already ask; now you are learning to ask well. That feels smaller, but it takes just as much learning.

blocks.x: Learners who read slowing progress as low ability often reduce their effort, producing the stagnation they feared.

body: Purpose: to explain diminishing visible returns. Content: a short, steep staircase labelled with beginner abilities beside a long, gentle ramp with small flags marking intermediate abilities. Style: clean line drawing. Board version: steps and a sloping line.

items: None needed; this is a whole-class explanation.

blocks.x: The board drawing, copied into notebooks.

pts: The intermediate plateau is a well-documented point of high learner attrition across many language-learning contexts.
Unit 22's motivation and self-efficacy research is especially relevant here — perceived lack of progress erodes both.
Proactively addressing this risk is more effective than waiting for visible disengagement to respond to it.

v: Class register; homework record; a short learner survey

items: Each month, note three signals: homework completion, voluntary participation, and learners’ comments about progress.
Give a short four-question survey with names, so that you can follow up (see model language).
Mark learners whose signals have dropped for two months in a row.
Plan a short individual conversation with each of them within a fortnight.
Record what you tried and whether the signals recovered.
Discuss the survey results with colleagues who teach the same learners other subjects.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A four-question survey (written for this book), answered on a scale of 1–4:

lines: I am making progress in English this term.
I know what I need to do to improve.
English lessons have been interesting recently.
I remember why English is useful to me.

blocks.x: A falling score on the first question alongside a steady score on the last suggests a learner who still values English but cannot see progress. That learner needs evidence (points 1 and 4) more than persuasion.

body: Purpose: to show proactive monitoring. Content: a simple dashboard with three small gauges (homework, participation, confidence) for one class; one gauge is dipping and a teacher is making a note. Style: calm infographic, not alarming. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Forms (free) for the survey; Google Sheets (free) to track monthly results.

blocks.x: A paper survey with tick boxes and a monthly tally in the teaching journal.

pts: Unit 42's portfolio approach is especially valuable here, making otherwise invisible development tangible over time.
Can-do checklists at this level should include nuanced, sociolinguistic and discourse-level descriptors, not just basic survival skills.
Comparing current work against work from several months earlier often reveals more progress than a learner perceives day to day.

v: The portfolio (Unit 42); a list of B1–B2 can-do statements

items: Show learners their old can-do checklist (for example ‘I can introduce myself’) and ask whether it still describes their goals.
Introduce a new list with discourse-level and sociolinguistic descriptors (see model language).
Learners rate themselves on each statement: ‘not yet’, ‘with help’, ‘on my own’.
For each ‘on my own’, they must point to evidence in their portfolio.
Repeat the rating every six weeks and add the date.
Learners write a can-do statement of their own for something they want to do outside school.
Support: give three statements only, each with a model example.
Challenge: learners comment briefly on the evidence for one statement.

blocks.x: Intermediate can-do statements (written for this book, in the spirit of the CEFR Companion Volume, Council of Europe 2020):

lines: I can tell a story with a beginning, a problem and an ending, using words like ‘suddenly’ and ‘in the end’.
I can say I disagree politely, for example ‘I see what you mean, but…’.
I can change how I write for a friend and for the Principal.

blocks.x: These name progress that a beginner checklist cannot see.

body: Purpose: to show can-do statements that match intermediate learning. Content: a notebook checklist; old statements faded, new ones in fresh ink with dated ticks. Style: handwritten, personal. Board version: a table with three columns.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for a printable checklist.
Council of Europe CEFR website (free) for the Companion Volume descriptors.

blocks.x: A handwritten checklist glued inside the notebook cover.

pts: Introducing new task types, genres, and content at this stage counters the sense of repetitive, static practice.
This connects to Tier II's broader emphasis on task-based, project-based and content-integrated variety.
Novelty itself has motivational value, independent of the specific skill being practised.

v: The scheme of work for one term (Unit 14)

items: List the task types in your scheme of work for the last six weeks.
Mark any type used three or more times in a row.
Replace at least two repeats with a new genre, task type or content area from the menu (see model language).
Keep the language aim the same where possible; change the vehicle.
Invite learners to propose one new task type for the next unit.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A menu of alternatives drawn from Part II:

lines: Instead of another comprehension passage: a jigsaw reading (Unit 34) or a graded reader circle (Unit 31).
Instead of another composition: a podcast script or a short project (Unit 36).
Instead of another textbook topic: a science or social science theme taught through English (Unit 37).

blocks.x: A class that practised narrative tenses through three textbook stories might instead retell grandparents’ folk tales in English for a class anthology: the same aim, a new experience.

body: Purpose: to show variety without losing focus. Content: a flag labelled ‘Language aim’ with roads leading to it from a microphone, a stage, a book and a science beaker. Style: bright map. Board version: a star with four arrows pointing to it.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shared bank of task ideas across a department.

blocks.x: A ‘task menu’ chart pinned in the staff room.

pts: Break the broad, distant goal of 'fluency' into shorter, more immediately achievable micro-goals.
This connects to Unit 22's self-efficacy research — frequent, specific success experiences sustain motivation better than distant ones.
Micro-goals also give more frequent opportunities for the visible-progress evidence this poster's earlier cards discuss.

items: Ask learners to write their big goal, for example ‘I want to speak fluently’.
Show how to break it into a goal for this week: specific, small and checkable.
Learners write one micro-goal on a card, with a date and a way of checking.
At the end of the week, learners tick, cross or adjust the goal with a partner.
Collect the ticked cards in the portfolio as evidence of success.
Learners share micro-goals in groups of four and check each other the following week.
Support: provide a sentence frame: ‘This week I will… I will know I have done it when…’.
Challenge: learners plan a four-week sequence of micro-goals.

blocks.x: From a distant goal to micro-goals (written for this book):

lines: Big goal: Speak English fluently.
Micro-goal 1: This week I will use three new phrases for giving opinions in class discussions.
Micro-goal 2: This week I will describe my day in English to my cousin in Hubballi on a phone call, for two minutes.

blocks.x: Short loops give frequent, specific successes, which Bandura (1997) identifies as the strongest source of self-efficacy.

body: Figure 47.6 Small flags on a long road

Purpose: to show micro-goals as frequent milestones. Content: a winding road towards a distant mountain labelled ‘Fluency’, with small flags every few steps, each flag a ticked card. Style: encouraging, simple. Board version: a line with many short ticks.

items: Google Keep (free) for learners with phones to record and tick goals.

blocks.x: Paper goal cards in an envelope inside the portfolio.

body: Keep micro-goals behavioural rather than evaluative. ‘I will use three opinion phrases’ can be checked; ‘I will speak better’ cannot. Learners need to be able to say ‘yes, I did it’ without waiting for the teacher’s verdict.

pts: Revisit the motivation type identified in Unit 2 — instrumental or integrative — and reconnect current work to it explicitly.
A learner who has lost sight of their original reason for learning is more vulnerable to plateau-stage discouragement.
This is a brief, low-cost check-in with high potential motivational value at this specific stage.

v: The needs analysis from the start of the course (Unit 2)

items: Return learners’ original needs analysis or ‘Why English?’ answers.
Learners read what they wrote and underline their main reason.
They decide whether it is still true, has changed, or has been forgotten.
They write one sentence connecting their reason to something they did in English this month.
Learners interview an adult who uses English at work and report back.
Support: provide reason cards to choose from (exams, jobs, travel, films, talking to relatives abroad).
Challenge: learners write about how their reason has changed.

lines: My reason: I want to become a nurse. This month: I wrote instructions for making ORS, and nurses need to explain things clearly.
My reason: I want to watch cricket commentary. This month: I followed a whole over of commentary without subtitles.

blocks.x: Gardner (1985) distinguished instrumental reasons (exams, jobs) from integrative ones (connecting with people and cultures). Dörnyei (2009) later argued that a vivid image of one’s future English-using self is itself a motivator. Either way, the reason works only if learners see it in their present work.

body: Purpose: to show the link between present effort and original purpose. Content: a learner doing homework, with a thread running from her notebook to a thought bubble showing her future self as a nurse. Style: warm, personal. Board version: a stick figure and a thought bubble joined by a line.

items: None needed; this is a reflection task.

blocks.x: The original needs analysis sheet, kept in the portfolio.

pts: Set realistic expectations about the plateau before learners reach it, rather than only responding once discouragement has set in.
A brief, honest conversation about this pattern early in a B1-level course can meaningfully reduce its later impact.
This connects to Unit 2's ongoing needs-analysis principle — expectations are part of what an effective needs analysis should manage.

v: 20 minutes at the start of an intermediate course
A graph drawing; the staircase and ramp (point 2)

items: In the first or second week of a B1 course, draw the two-line graph from Figure 47.1.
Explain: ‘At some point this year you will feel stuck. Almost everyone does. It does not mean you have stopped learning.’
Ask learners what they usually do when they feel stuck in a sport, a game or music practice.
Together, list three things the class will do when the plateau arrives (see model language).
Invite a former learner, now in Class 11 or college, to describe how they felt at this stage and what helped.
Support: explain the idea briefly in the home language.
Challenge: learners write a ‘letter to my future stuck self’.

blocks.x: A class agreement (written for this book):

lines: When we feel stuck, we will: (1) compare our work with work from three months ago; (2) set one small goal for the week; (3) remind ourselves why we are learning English.
T: Have you ever practised a song or a bowling action and felt you were not getting better? Did you get better in the end?
S1: Yes, but slowly.
T: English at this stage is the same.

blocks.x: Expectation-setting is part of ongoing needs analysis (Unit 2): learners’ beliefs about how fast they should improve are as important to manage as their goals.

body: Purpose: to show prevention rather than cure. Content: learners on a mountain path, a teacher pointing ahead to a signpost reading ‘Flat for a while: keep walking’. Style: friendly, adventurous. Board version: a path with a signpost.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for a class agreement poster.

blocks.x: The class agreement on chart paper on the wall.

body: With one B1 class this month, do ‘Then and now’ (point 1) and ask each learner to set one micro-goal (point 6). A fortnight later, repeat the survey from point 3 and compare the first item.

dek: Unit 47 of 100: progress that felt rapid at beginner level often slows and flattens through the intermediate stage — a well-documented pattern with real methodological responses.

aims.x: A class that raced through its first years of English reaches B1 and seems to stop. Learners say ‘I am not improving’, and some quietly give up. This unit explains why progress at the intermediate level feels slower than it is, and offers practical ways of making it visible, varying the challenge and keeping learners’ reasons for learning alive.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain the intermediate plateau as a feature of language development rather than a failure of ability or effort;
describe why the same amount of learning feels smaller at B1–B2 than at A1–A2;
recognize early signs of plateau-stage discouragement and respond before learners disengage;
use portfolios, before-and-after comparisons and advanced can-do checklists to make progress visible;
vary task types, genres and content to counter a sense of repetitive practice;
help learners break the distant goal of ‘fluency’ into short, achievable micro-goals;
reconnect current classwork to learners’ original reasons for learning English;
prepare learners for the plateau honestly before they reach it.

why: Why this matters. Many learners abandon language study specifically at this plateau, mistaking a normal developmental pattern for a sign they've stopped improving or aren't capable.

background.x: Jack C. Richards (2008) describes the intermediate plateau: learners can survive in English, but they rely on familiar words and structures and find it hard to move towards the richer, more precise use expected at advanced levels. Part of the difficulty is real; part of it is perception. At beginner level each new structure unlocks something new: asking the way, telling the time, describing a family. At intermediate level new learning refines what learners can already partly do, such as choosing argue rather than say, or softening a disagreement. These gains matter, but they are hard to notice day to day.

Perception matters because motivation depends on it. Zoltán Dörnyei (2001) shows that motivation is not a fixed trait: it has to be generated, maintained and protected, and the teacher has a large part in each stage. Albert Bandura’s (1997) research on self-efficacy identifies mastery experiences, the learner’s own evidence of success, as its most powerful source. If learners cannot see their progress, they lose that evidence, and with it their belief that effort pays off. Unit 22 introduced self-efficacy; this unit applies it where it is most tested. Goal-setting research adds a further point: specific, near and challenging goals sustain effort better than vague or distant ones (Locke and Latham 2002).

In India the plateau often coincides with the secondary years, when examination pressure rises and texts become longer and more abstract. NEP 2020 emphasizes competency-based learning, regular formative assessment and the joy of learning, and NCF 2023 asks for assessment that shows learners what they can do rather than only what they got wrong (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020; NCERT 2023). A multilingual learner who reads the same story in Kannada and in English, noticing how much more of the English she now understands, is gathering the evidence of progress that keeps motivation alive.

items: Before-and-after comparison. Learners’ annotated pairs of work, showing three identified improvements each.
Updated can-do checklist. A dated B1–B2 checklist with portfolio evidence for each ‘on my own’ rating.
Micro-goal record. Four weeks of goal cards, with ticks and adjustments.
Teacher monitoring record. A term’s early-warning data for one class, with notes on responses and outcomes.
When did you last feel stuck in learning something? What helped you move on?
How do your learners know they are improving? What evidence do they see?
Which task types have you used most often this term? Which could you replace?
Do your can-do checklists still match what your intermediate learners are learning?
How often do you remind learners of their own reasons for learning English?
Have you ever told a class, in advance, that a plateau is coming?

terms.def: A description of what a learner can do in a language, as in the CEFR, used for setting goals, self-assessment and describing levels; for example, ‘I can write a short email inviting a friend.’
Helping learners form realistic beliefs about how fast they will progress, for example preparing them for the slower gains of the intermediate plateau so that they do not lose motivation.
The image of the person a learner would like to become as a user of the second language, such as a confident English-speaking engineer. It is a key source of motivation (Dörnyei 2009).
Motivation to learn a language for practical benefits, such as passing an examination or getting a job (Gardner and Lambert 1972).
Motivation to learn a language because of interest in, or a wish to connect with, its speakers and their culture (Gardner and Lambert 1972).
A stage at which learners, usually at intermediate level, feel they are no longer making progress despite continued study (Richards 2008).
A learner’s own direct experience of succeeding at a task, identified by Bandura (1997) as the most powerful source of self-efficacy; visible progress records help learners notice such experiences.
A small, specific and achievable learning target, such as learning five phrases for agreeing, into which a distant goal like ‘fluency’ can be broken so that learners see steady progress.

A person’s belief in their ability to succeed at a particular task (Bandura 1977). Learners with higher self-efficacy in English persist longer and take more risks; achievable tasks and specific praise help to build it.
